Movies Review The Visitor review – existential Lithuania-set homecoming drama leaves everything in limbo This portrait by Vytautas Katkus of a man contemplating his recent fatherhood and his own father is steeped in ennui and ends up drifting Phil Hoad Mon 24 Aug 2026 06.26 EDT Last modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 06.27 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A t one point in this Nordic-Baltic homecoming film, Danielius (Darius Šilėnas) refuses an invite for beachfront karaoke, preferring to watch from behind a polythene partition. At another, a neighbour glimpses him exercising across the courtyard, through the window of the flat in an end-of-summer Lithuanian resort that Danielius is trying to sell. Having returned from Norway to settle up accounts, this prodigal son is often holding the world at arm’s length – and director Vytautas Katkus does his best to help him with this distanced technique in this quizzical and faintly existential drama. Little tangible is disclosed. Danielius is a thirtysomething father who skipped the funeral of his own dad the year before. Preparing the flat to go on the market, he walks the dog of his neighbour, Vismante (Vismantė Ruzgaitė), hangs speculatively at beach gatherings and falls asleep in pine forests. Ice-cream is eaten at every available opportunity. He’s not alienated exactly, but somewhat out of step. As he looks for new anchorage, even the film seems to question whether Danielius has sufficient main character energy: it periodically drifts to follow another resident, Tomas (Rokas Siaurusaitis), who is caring for his grandmother over the way. Given Katkus’s cinematography background, it’s not surprising that this smalltown ennui comes gracefully shot, with stray snippets of quirk, like the fairground diplodocus poking its head over the treetops as Danielius arrives. But with much of The Visitor’s long runtime devoted to simply surveilling this entropic purgatory and little else, it leaves it until late before openly broaching the matter of its protagonist’s diffidence. Is it because of guilt for returning too late? Or tied up with feelings about his own recent fatherhood? Or just common nostalgia about his old family life? All of the above, possibly. With the paternal issue apparently settled by a strange request over breakfast to Vismante’s father, Katkus – steadfast in his love of the mid-shot thus far – abandons his previous reserve. Where a character being gifted a red lifeguard beach inflatable prompted a diegetic burst of the Baywatch theme tune in the first half, the second half sees the film break with realism almost entirely for another seafront musical number. If not as stridently deadpan and stylised as the likes of Aki Kaurismäki, it brings gentler, intriguing notes of absurdism and human warmth to this seaside haven. https://www.bursa.ro/romanian-academy-an.text: The Romanian Academy and the Academy of Sciences of Moldova will jointly mark Romanian Language Day today, through a festive session organized simultaneously in Bucharest and Chisinau. The event will include lectures dedicated to the evolution and use of the Romanian language, its cultural and identity status, as well as the impact of artificial intelligence on the language. The event will take place from 11:00, in the Aula of the Romanian Academy and in the Sala Azurie of the Academy of Sciences of Moldova and is organized in partnership with the National Museum of Romanian Literature. The opening remarks will be delivered by the President of the Romanian Academy, Marius Andruh, present in Chisinau, and by the President of the Academy of Sciences of Moldova, Ion Tighineanu. *Lectures on the evolution and status of the Romanian language The festive program will bring together members of the Romanian Academy and specialists from its research institutes, who will address topics regarding the evolution, use and identity status of the Romanian language. The President of the Romanian Academic Council, Ioan-Aurel Pop, and the Vice President of the Romanian Academy, Mircea Dumitru, will speak about the relationship between language and nation and about the role of the national language in the European cultural space. Prof. Rodica Zafiu, corresponding member of the Romanian Academy, will address the relationship between the spontaneous use of the language by speakers and the cultural authority of the linguistic norm. In turn, Fr. Dr. Bogdan Tătaru Cazaban, scientific researcher at the Institute of History of Religions of the Romanian Academy, will present the liturgical sources of the literary Romanian language. *Romanian Language in the Age of Artificial Intelligence The Bucharest session will conclude with a lecture dedicated to the situation of the Romanian language in the context of the development of artificial intelligence, given by the Director General of the National Museum of Romanian Literature, Ioan Cristescu. The program will continue with a poetry recital given by actor Marius Bodochi. Public participation in the Romanian Academy Hall is free, and the festive session will be broadcast live on the Romanian Academy's YouTube channel. *Romanian Language Day, established in Romania in 2013 According to the Romanian Academy, the events dedicated to this day are part of the institution's mission to cultivate and standardize the national language, through the development of dictionaries, grammars, anthologies, studies and research, as well as through cultural activities. Romanian Language Day is celebrated annually on August 31. The date marks the moment in 1989 when the Parliament in Chisinau voted the law on the return of the Romanian language and Latin script in the Republic of Moldova. In 1990, the Republic of Moldova established the same date for the celebration of "Our Language", and in Romania, August 31 was consecrated as Romanian Language Day by a decision of the Parliament adopted in 2013. Photograph: James D Morgan/Getty Images View image in fullscreen EVs are being taken up as a cost-of-living measure, experts say, with the ongoing fuel crisis an accelerating factor but ‘not the starting gun’. Photograph: James D Morgan/Getty Images Electric vehicles An EV sold every 100 seconds: Australian demand for electric cars more than doubles A record 157,957 new EVs were sold nationally between January and June, according to the Electric Vehicle Council Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Donna Lu Assistant editor, climate, environment and science Tue 29 Sep 2026 22.02 EDT Last modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 22.03 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Australians are buying electric vehicles at record levels, with sales more than doubling year on year and occurring at a rate equivalent to one EV sold every 100 seconds. A record 157,957 EV sales occurred between January and June – an 117% increase on the same period last year, according to a new report released by the Electric Vehicle Council. Comparatively, petrol and diesel vehicle sales decreased by 14% year on year, according to the council’s chief executive, Julie Delvecchio. Electric car owners could save hundreds of dollars a year under the solar sharer scheme. Here’s how Read more EVs accounted for one in four new vehicles sold in the first half of the year, up 12.1% from the first six months of 2025, the state of EVs report said. “EVs are being taken up as a cost-of-living measure by households across Australia,” Delvecchio said of the rise, noting that the ongoing fuel crisis was an accelerating factor but was “not the starting gun”. “It exposed the value of the policy work that had already been done – and made the lower running costs and energy security benefits of EVs much more immediate for Australian households,” she said. The new figures include about 104,000 battery electric vehicles and 54,000 plug-in hybrids. As of June, there were 612,000 EVs in the national vehicle fleet. “We are well on track to hit the target of 1 million EVs on Australian roads by next year,” said Aman Gaur, the head of policy and advocacy at the EV Council. The Australian Capital Territory, where 44% of new cars registered are electric, retained its crown as the nation’s EV capital. Tarneit, in Melbourne’s west, was the individual postcode with the highest uptake. A key driver of the growing uptake has been the national vehicle efficiency standard, which requires carmakers to supply new vehicles that meet an average per-kilometre emissions target. The standard had “substantially increased the options and the price competitiveness of EVs”, with nearly 200 EV models available in 2026, Gaur said. The council is pushing for the federal government to extend the standard beyond 2029, to align with the government’s 2035 emissions reduction target . Subdued take up of electric trucks Charging infrastructure had largely kept pace with growing EV demand, the report found, with the number of public charging locations growing to 4,268 across the country. While Australia was no longer a global laggard compared with other electric car markets, buses and cars were “roaring ahead” of electric trucks and vans, for which sales continued to be less than 1% of their respective markets, Gaur said. “Every truck that is electric is an upgrade to Australia’s energy security,” Delvecchio said. “We’ve barely touched the sides on that transition.” The report also found the federal, ACT and NSW governments’ EV policies were “top of the class, while South Australia, Queensland, Tasmania and Northern Territory have gone backwards”. “Queensland and the Northern Territory are … moving to back to fossil fuels rather than trying to electrify their transport systems,” Gaur said. “The most disappointing example of this was when the Queensland government recently invested in 630 diesel buses . “The diesel buses will be on Queensland roads until the end of the next decade, and they will certainly be polluting the air in Brisbane when the Olympics are held.” Explore more on these topics Electric vehicles Transport news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Antarctic winter sea ice falls to third-lowest level on record as scientists warn of ‘now problem’ How one woman’s Tesla was remotely controlled – and used to harass her – by an abusive ex-partner Electric car owners could save hundreds of dollars a year under the solar sharer scheme. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Illustration: Retouch by GMN Imaging and Getty View image in fullscreen Illustration: Retouch by GMN Imaging and Getty France France’s other schools problem – the teens violently smashing up their old primaries: ‘They think it’s not worthy of respect – so they trash it’ The phenomenon of pupils wrecking equipment and setting fire to classrooms predates the current crisis. Is it rooted in poverty, social media peer pressure – or just plain boredom? Phil Hoad Sun 11 Oct 2026 01.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google L ike most French primaries on Wednesdays, Marcel Pagnol school, in the eastern suburbs of Lyon, was shut on 19 June 2024. But at 6.30pm that evening, two boys turned up late for school – by two years. Former pupils there, the 13-year-olds struggled to break through the crispy lattice of the front-door window with a garden fork and a broom. Using a window-breaker, they finally created an opening large enough to force their way in without hurting themselves. What happened next is captured in a video the pair subsequently posted on Snapchat . Once inside they prowl the classrooms, corridors and canteen, slinging around scooters and smashing up computer equipment, setting off fire extinguishers and upending furniture. They help themselves to pouches of Capri‑Sun from the fridge: “I don’t give a fuck – I’m taking the lot.” The boy not filming sets small fires as they move through the building, squirting each one with a little jet of lighter fuel. “I love what’s happening here!” says his accomplice. “I love fire.” But the exhilaration soon turns to panic. With a thick black canopy of smoke creeping along the ceiling of the main corridor, they realise it’s time to go: “Come on, come on, there’s smoke everywhere. Fuck, I can’t see a thing!” They’re soon scarpering into the surrounding streets in broad daylight, the cameraman sipping his Capri-Sun as a column of smoke rises from the school, and police cars converge on the site. It’s a pattern of carnivalesque destruction – like the mass burning of cars during urban riots – that seems distinctively French The Marcel Pagnol arson was perhaps the most serious incident of a phenomenon that has swept the whole of France in recent years: comprehensive trashings of school premises that go well beyond isolated acts of vandalism. There were at least 15 cases in 2025; a similar number in 2024. The damage inflicted on at least 24 high schools across the country during this month’s student protests seem to some extent to fit this pattern – though these actions are fuelled by particular shared grievances, including dilapidated facilities and endemic staff shortages. Perhaps attacks on schools like Marcel Pagnol should have served as canaries in the coalmine for rising tension, resentment and nihilistic feeling among students towards the institutions supposedly there to guarantee their future. Such events crop up in other countries, but here they seem to fit a pattern of carnivalesque destruction – like the mass burning of cars during urban riots – that seems distinctively French. In a sense, trashings are the country’s equivalent of school shootings in America – though obviously far less deadly and generally perpetrated by groups, not loners. To highlight a few: smashed computers and broken windows at Rabelais secondary school in Vitry-sur-Seine in March 2024, the fourth break-in in six months; graffiti of a swastika, an anarchist symbol and anti‑Rassemblement National (RN) slogans left behind by ideologically confused hooligans at André Malraux secondary school in Baignes-Sainte-Radegonde, near Bordeaux; “ Foke les profs ” (Fuck the teachers) scrawled amid the devastation at Jean Moulin primary school in Montgeron, on Paris’s southern edge; one primary school and two nursery schools laid waste to in 2025 in working-class neighbourhoods of the Provençal city of Arles. View image in fullscreen Rabelais secondary school in Vitry-sur-Seine, a commune in the south-eastern suburbs of Paris, suffered four break-ins in six months in 2024. Photograph: Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP/Getty Images In a strikingly large number of cases, it is primary schools that are attacked. When the perpetrators are caught, they are often children of early secondary-school age returning to wreak havoc. In many cases, they’re trashing the same schools in which their younger siblings are still taught. “My sister’s got school here tomorrow,” crows one of the intruders in the video from École Marcel Pagnol. On the one hand, there’s a festive misrule in such acts: the paint-lashed walls, the upturned shelves, the rainbow debris of playbricks strewn across play areas. On the other, there’s an aspect of psychological self-harm in play, akin to destroying the family home, that’s also visible in this month’s lycée attacks. It’s hard to square this beguiling clash of motives. What’s clear is the impact on the surrounding community. Two years after the attack, on a humid June Monday morning, the final one before the summer holidays, pupils and parents are ambling up to Marcel Pagnol to start the school day. It’s situated in the suburb of Meyzieu, a relatively well-off and unremarkable commuter dormitory of Lyon set in the arable land that sprawls towards the city airport. The school’s cream, two-storey blocks have been restored to pristine condition – at a cost of €1.9m to the Meyzieu municipality (partly covered by insurance). But the attack caused a real sense of violation. “I’m sad,” six-year-old Lino told reporters from TV station BFM right after the arson. “All my drawings burned.” And the feeling still lingers. “They set the school alight with a toxic product,” says Evan, a boy of eight or nine with thumbs inside his backpack strap. “There were flames.” Audrey Granger, a member of the parents’ association, points out the children had to process seeing their charred drawings on the walls, the burnt exercise books. She didn’t tell her daughter, who attended the nursery school next door, what had happened. “We wanted to leave her in her own little bubble,” she says. “It was as if you left your office and someone said to you: you have no right to come back,” Juliane Fauriat, the headteacher, says. “You didn’t anticipate it, you have to leave everything behind, which is very difficult.” Her staff removed salvageable equipment in crates provided by the town hall; two traumatised teachers walked out with empty boxes from their entirely burnt-out classrooms. Two sources tell me that the break-in at Louise-Michel was in response to online ‘challenges’ teenagers set each on social networks The following academic year, Marcel Pagnol’s 240 pupils were housed in prefab annexes on an empty field opposite – a novelty for some of them. But with the canteen severely damaged, lunchtime had to be split between two other school sites: one a bus ride away for the younger children; another 15 minutes’ walk away for the older ones. “They had to do it in the heat of summer and in winter,” says Sabrina, a mum in a flowery dress lingering at the end of the school run. “Can you imagine? My daughter was crying sometimes – she was always running late.” The two 13-year-old perpetrators – one of whom shows his face in the video and names the other – were caught almost immediately. They had no criminal record and were unknown to the police; one had an “irreproachable” academic record, says Sandrine Carroz, a coordinator with the municipality’s education services. The other was going through a “fragile period, where communication with his parents was complicated”. But there had been nothing to indicate he might erupt in this way. Sylvie Normand, the deputy mayor of Meyzieu, the area served by École Marcel Pagnol, says: “I think these were young people who dared each other to do something and who came up with a bad idea, which went through their heads without them thinking about the consequences.” The online lynch mob assembled: “Give them another chance – they were just expressing their anger at having to retake year 3 for the fifth time” is one sarcastic comment under a news report posted on YouTube. Others hint at the societal and ethnic tensions inflaming French public life – heightened in Lyon, which is a centre of far-right activity: “Kick them out of the country, along with the parents who are taking our family allowances.” (Based on the name mentioned by one of the boys in the videos, and their slang, many commenters assumed they had immigrant origins; their identities as minors are of course protected by law.) Tiffany Joncour, the local RN candidate, was quickly on the scene to film a video declaring: “It’s time to stop these delinquents who act with impunity and spoil all our lives.” The pair received four-month suspended sentences and were placed under special court supervision for 18 months. The municipality agreed with the two families to send their siblings to other schools. Over the road from École Marcel Pagnol, boulangerie worker Miriam is more circumspect than most: “It could have been my child – because you never know, especially with the influence of social networks these days. I hope it knocks some sense into them. And their families, too, because they have to take some responsibility.” As the Marcel Pagnol perpetrators are minors, it’s impossible to ask them the crucial question: what led them to break down the front door on that day? But perhaps it’s possible to pursue a second one: what do these messy tremors from the teenage subconscious collectively say about French society? ‘T hey think it’s not worthy of respect – so they trash it.” Outside Louise-Michel primary school in Arles earlier this year in March, parent Etienne Becker suggests it was a fundamental disdain for national institutions that led four youths, aged between 11 and 13, to break and enter and do approximately €30,000 worth of damage there in July 2025. He’s dropping his six-year-old son off at a squat, tan complex with a barracks-like air. Louise‑Michel is on the edge of Griffeuille, a marginalised neighbourhood dominated by hal‑rendered blocks of public housing in which 57% live below the poverty line. The values of the French state – “Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité” – are displayed on insignia outside almost all the country’s schools (as Becker points out, they are curiously absent at Louise-Michel). It’s in places like Griffeuille where it’s easiest to assume that school trashings may be a form of aggression, conscious or not, towards how these lofty ideals translate in practice. Éric Debarbieux, a veteran researcher who formerly directed the International Observatory of Violence in School and has advised the French government, corroborates this, suggesting that for the attackers, “it’s a way of saying: schools don’t keep their promises. The values displayed aren’t the same as the values in reality.” That might explain why this form of mayhem occurs so consistently in France, where schools are adorned with the livery and rhetoric of the Fifth Republic. But it’s hard to exactly quantify it, as the national annual statistics on school violence don’t list incident numbers. Only a percentage breakdown for property damage (3% in primary schools and 4% in secondary schools/sixth-form colleges in 2024-25) among total incidents reported is given. Verbal and physical violence are far more common (45% and 34% of incidents reported in primary schools). Just because school trashings are statistically less frequent doesn’t mean they aren’t significant. It’s precisely their intensely visible character – the unbridled violation of a public space – that gives them power. Debarbieux emphasises the particular character of these acts: “They’re a kind of game. There’s possibly a kind of group jubilation behind them: it’s these children’s manner of expressing themselves.” He believes such incidents have been occurring at least since the 1990s – when statistics on French school violence first began – and have steadily risen since. The more you ‘protect’ schools from the surrounding neighbourhood, they more they look like the enemy As in Lyon, silence has gathered around the series of incidents that hit the east side of Arles last year. The municipality won’t comment, and one teacher I encounter says they have been forbidden by the education board from talking about them to the press. The parents outside Louise-Michel speculate about the motivations of the invaders, who were caught after tripping an alarm and in some cases were forced by their parents to participate in the clean-up. But no one here today knows their identity, or anything specific. The same is true at Victoria Lyles nursery school in the neighbourhood of Trébon, 2km to the north. It was ransacked, along with a nearby primary school, by eight secondary school pupils from the area in February 2025, who were caught on security cameras and convicted of vandalising school property. Again, some had younger siblings at Victoria Lyles; they urinated in the classrooms where pupils studied. Lazy brown mosquitoes swarm the parents picking up their offspring on this March lunchtime. A general air of incomprehension and resignation reigns regarding the break-in. “We were afraid for our children, as there isn’t any proper security here,” says one of a group of three mothers. Resources are strained in the commune; France’s largest by surface area, with lots of schools, but a low tax base. In the wake of the three 2025 trashings, the Arles municipality invested €650,000 in better security for the affected schools, including linking their alarms to a central surveillance centre. In the cornershop down the road, I’m told no one in Trébon will break the general “omertà” regarding the eight offenders. Neighbourhoods like this and Griffeuille are hotspots for the driving factors behind school violence. Laurent Mucchielli, a specialist in the sociology of delinquency at the French National Centre for Scientific Research, points out three key indicators for troublemakers: academic failure; coming from “poor or stigmatised” neighbourhoods; and difficulties within the family. But he insists the first is paramount: “Until they’re 18 years old, school is the essential structure of collective social integration for young people, what you might call the society of children. So academic failure is the first form of exclusion from society.” It’s not hard to see why such children might react by channelling their anger against the site of their humiliation. View image in fullscreen Bois d’Aulne secondary school in a suburb of Paris, where Samuel Paty was beheaded by an attacker in 2020 for showing pupils a caricature of the prophet Muhammad. Photograph: Anne-Christine Poujoulat/AFP/Getty Images Mucchielli stresses that overall levels of school violence in France have remained stable since the 1990s – counter to the media and political narrative of feral youth. He also downplays the effect of social media, saying it doesn’t create new forms of behaviour. But it’s clear that it shapes some individual incidents; providing not just, as in École Marcel Pagnol, the means of dissemination, but also of incitement. Two sources tell me that the break-in at Louise-Michel was in response to online “challenges” teenagers set each on social networks; one of them, from Arles town hall, says the offenders came from outside Griffeuille to vandalise the school. But it’s not easy to track this social network peer pressure, often posted as ephemeral Snapchat or TikTok stories, with generic, algorithm-bait hashtags. Normand, the deputy mayor speculates that online content has a desensitising effect: “They see stuff like that, it’s virtual, but then they identify with it and they make the leap.” Speaking on condition of anonymity, two teachers who have had to deal with such incidents agree on another explanation that pre-dates 21st-century social media: boredom. Az amerikai közvetítők a háború utáni biztonsági garanciákra és Ukrajna újjáépítésére is igyekeznek összpontosítani, miközben Kijev továbbra is elutasítja, hogy lemondjon a teljes Donbaszról. Kushner és Steve Witkoff amerikai különmegbízott csütörtökön Moszkvában tárgyal Vlagyimir Putyin orosz elnökkel, majd Írországban Volodimir Zelenszkij ukrán elnökkel egyeztetnek. Kushner szerint az európai országokat is be kell vonni a béketárgyalásokba. Az orosz delegáció ugyanakkor Abu-Dzabiban nem volt hajlandó találkozni az európai és NATO-képviselőkkel. Az ukrán küldöttséget képviselő David Arahamija nehéznek nevezte az egyeztetéseket, de úgy vélte, azok lendületet adhatnak az év végéig elérendő megállapodásnak. Andrij Szibiha ukrán külügyminiszter közben közölte, hogy Kijev továbbra is várja Moszkva válaszát a fekete-tengeri gabonaszállítások biztonságát célzó tűzszüneti javaslatra.
